 Mother gets land from government and after her death, son seeks patta transfer as her legal heir; but authorities initiate eviction proceedings; why Madras HC denied him relief

 Medium

 Print The court clarified that legal heirs of an original allottee cannot claim a patta transfer if they do not meet the eligibility requirements. (Image for representative purpose only) Your mother has been allotted land by the government and after she passes, you claim right to it as a legal heir. Are you entitled to the land or can the government ask you to vacate the property? A recent Madras High Court ruling highlights why people who receive government-granted land must comply with the conditions attached to the allotment. Failure to do so could result in their children losing the property, even if they claim it through inheritance. In a November 4, 2026, ruling, the Madras High Court held that Grama Natham land cannot automatically pass to heirs when the conditions of the original grant have been violated. What the case is about
 A man’s mother had been assigned Grama Natham land. After her death, the man continued to occupy the property and applied for the patta to be transferred in his favour as her legal heir. While his application was pending, revenue authorities initiated proceedings under the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905. The Land Revenue Inspector issued a notice under Section 7, followed by a notice under Section 6 issued by the Revenue Tahsildar. The man challenged both notices before the Madras High Court. The mother had received land under the Grama Natham rules administered by the Tamil Nadu government. Grama Natham land is government-owned land which is allocated to landless poor people for housing and public use. Such grants, however, come with specific conditions. If these are breached, the government can then reclaim the land. The authorities sought to evict the man on the ground that his mother had violated the conditions governing the grant. Challenging the move in court, he argued that the government could not remove him from the property because he had inherited it from his mother, despite its classification as Grama Natham land. The man’s counsel argued that the Tahsildar had failed to consider the explanation submitted in response to the notice. He also contended that Grama Natham land did not vest with the government and that the authorities therefore lacked jurisdiction to initiate eviction proceedings. The state government opposed the petition. Its counsel argued that Grama Natham land could be regulated under Revenue Standing Orders 21 and 26 and assigned to eligible landless poor persons for residential purposes. The government further submitted that the original assignment was conditional and that compliance with its terms required examination. The state also argued that the man should have pursued the statutory appeal available under Section 10 of the 1905 Act instead of approaching the Madras High Court directly. Why Madras High Court did not give relief
 The Madras High Court noted that the man’s principal argument was that the government had allotted land to his mother and, following her death, he had applied for a patta transfer as her legal heir. Instead of approving his application, the authorities rejected it and initiated steps to evict him. The court clarified that legal heirs of an original allottee, who was the man’s mother in this case, cannot claim a patta transfer if they do not meet the eligibility requirements. It held that government land allotted subject to conditions cannot automatically pass to heirs as inherited property. The land continues to belong to the government, and its allotment remains governed by the terms laid down in the Revenue Standing Orders. Following the death of the original allottee, the authorities can examine whether the legal heirs qualify to receive government land free of cost. If they are found ineligible, the property can be allotted to another eligible poor person after following the procedures prescribed under the Revenue Standing Orders. Asha Kiran Sharma, partner at King Stubb and Kasiva, told ET that the man lost the case for three reasons. The first was his failure to file a statutory appeal under Section 10 of the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905. Second was that he relied on the argument that Grama Natham land did not vest in the government and, consequently, the Tahsildar could not invoke the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905. The third reason was the High Court’s finding that land granted subject to specific conditions does not automatically become hereditary property. Under Revenue Standing Orders 21 and 26, Grama Natham land is allotted to landless poor people, up to a prescribed extent, subject to certain conditions. When the original allottee dies, the authorities must determine whether the heirs meet the eligibility criteria. If they do not, the land can be allotted to another eligible poor person. The bench examined the legal position governing Grama Natham land and referred to earlier Madras High Court decisions, including S. Anbananthan v. The District Collector, Perambalur and Selvakumar v. The Additional Chief Secretary to Government . The court held that merely occupying Grama Natham land did not confer ownership rights. It observed: “Grama Natham lands may be occupied only under the authority of law and mere occupation of Grama Natham lands would not confer any ownership to an individual.” The bench also considered the nature of government land assignments. It explained that an assignment made subject to conditions does not automatically become hereditary property following the original assignee's death. The eligibility of legal heirs must be examined under the applicable rules. Paragraph 5 of the order expressly states: “In the present case, the assignee had violated the conditions.” The court therefore treated the violation as a finding in this particular case, rather than merely a possibility raised by the government. The Madras High Court recorded that the original assignee had violated the conditions attached to the patta. However, the judgment does not specify which particular condition was breached. The judgment also addressed the argument that Grama Natham land did not vest with the government. Relying on earlier decisions and the Revenue Standing Orders, the bench held that the government had the authority to regulate such land and take action against unauthorised occupation. The order stated: “The Revenue Standing Orders will have the force of law and further contemplates that the occupants of Grama Natham lands without authority of law are to be treated as encroachers and the Government is empowered to evict those encroachers by following the procedures as contemplated under the provisions of the Act, 1905.” The court also considered the availability of an alternative legal remedy. The man had not filed the statutory appeal contemplated under Section 10 of the Land Encroachment Act. The bench considered this omission significant because the original authority had relied on revenue documents and violations of the conditions attached to the assignment. Join conversation

 It observed: “Exhausting the efficacious alternate remedy contemplated under the Act, 1905 is of paramount importance.” The court consequently held that the challenge to the notices was not entertainable in the circumstances of the case. The ruling does not establish that every legal heir of a person holding an assigned residential plot is automatically ineligible for a patta transfer. Rather, the judgment emphasises that eligibility depends on the applicable assignment conditions and that challenges to revenue action must follow the prescribed legal procedures.
